title: Electricity: Magnetic and Heating Effects
subject: Science
description: Grade 8 NCERT Curiosity chapter 4: the magnetic effect of current and electromagnets, the heating effect and resistance, and how Voltaic, dry and rechargeable cells generate electricity.

questions.question: In Activity 4.1, what happens to the compass needle placed under the wire when the switch is moved to ON?
options: It deflects from its original direction
It spins continuously in circles
It points towards the electric cell
It stays exactly where it was before
questions.explanation: When current flows through the wire, the compass needle is deflected from its original direction; it does not spin continuously or point to the cell.

questions.question: When the switch in Activity 4.1 is moved back to OFF, the compass needle…
options: swings but settles pointing east
returns to its original direction
stays deflected at the same angle
deflects to the opposite side
questions.explanation: The magnetic effect exists only while current flows. When the current stops the effect disappears and the needle returns to where it pointed before.

questions.question: The deflection of a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire indicates that…
options: the compass needle has lost its magnetism
the cell is pushing the needle with static charge
the wire has a magnetic effect while current flows
the wire has become permanently magnetised
questions.explanation: The compass needle is a tiny magnet; it deflects only because the current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it. The wire is not permanently magnetised – the effect vanishes when current stops.

questions.question: The region around a magnet or a current-carrying wire where its magnetic effect can be felt is said to have a…
options: magnetic pole
electric circuit
magnetic core
magnetic field
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a magnetic field as the region around a magnet or current-carrying wire where its magnetic effect can be felt, for example by deflecting a compass needle.

questions.question: A thin cardboard sheet is placed between the current-carrying wire and the compass in Activity 4.1. What happens when the current flows?
options: The needle still deflects, since the effect acts through non-magnetic materials
The needle will not deflect, because cardboard blocks magnetic fields
The needle deflects only if the cardboard is wet and conducting
The needle deflects twice as much because cardboard concentrates it
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls from Grade 6 that a magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials kept in between, so cardboard does not block the deflection.

questions.question: Which statement about the magnetic effect of electric current is NOT correct?
options: Switching the current ON and OFF repeatedly deflects the needle each time
The magnetic field remains around the wire after current stops
A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around it
The compass needle is itself a tiny magnet that gets deflected
questions.explanation: The magnetic field disappears as soon as the current stops flowing – that is why the needle returns to its original direction. The other three statements are all made in the chapter.

questions.question: A compass needle near a wire deflects only while electric current is flowing through the wire.
questions.explanation: The deflection appears when current flows and disappears when it stops, showing the magnetic effect exists only during current flow.

questions.question: The magnetic effect of a current-carrying wire can be felt only if the compass actually touches the wire.
questions.explanation: The wire produces a magnetic field in the region around it, so a compass placed beneath (not touching) the wire is deflected.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the switch in the circuit of Activity 4.1?
options: To hold the wire above the cardboard
To protect the compass from heating
To start and stop the flow of current
To increase the strength of the cell
questions.explanation: Moving the switch between ON and OFF lets students start and stop the current while watching how the compass needle responds.

questions.question: Why is the longer wire in Activity 4.1 stretched between two nails slightly above the cardboard?
options: So the wire cools faster in the open air
So the wire does not short-circuit the cell
So the magnetic field is blocked by the board
So the compass can be placed just beneath the wire
questions.explanation: The wire is fixed slightly above the cardboard so that the magnetic compass can be placed beneath the wire between the two nails and observed.

questions.question: A student finds that the compass needle in Activity 4.1 does not deflect at all when the switch is ON. What is the most likely reason?
options: The circuit is broken somewhere, so no current flows
The cell is too strong for the compass to respond
The compass is not made of a magnetic material
The wire is too short to produce any magnetism
questions.explanation: The deflection depends on current actually flowing. If there is no deflection, the most likely cause is that current is not flowing because the circuit is incomplete. A stronger cell would give more deflection, not none.

questions.question: Which statements about the magnetic field produced by an electric current are correct?
options: It exists only while current flows
It is produced by any current-carrying conductor
It is stored in the wire after the cell is removed
It appears only when the wire is made of iron
questions.explanation: A magnetic field is produced around any conductor carrying current and disappears when the current stops. It is not stored, and it does not require an iron wire – the activity uses ordinary connecting wire.

questions.question: Which item in Activity 4.1 acts as the detector of the magnetic effect?
options: Cardboard base
Magnetic compass
Electric cell
Safety pin switch
questions.explanation: The magnetic compass needle, being a tiny magnet, deflects when a magnetic field is present and so detects the magnetic effect of the current.

questions.question: The phenomenon in which a conductor carrying current produces a magnetic field around it is known as the…
options: chemical effect of electric current
static effect of electric charges
magnetic effect of electric current
heating effect of electric current
questions.explanation: Production of a magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor is called the magnetic effect of electric current; the heating effect is the warming of a conductor.

questions.question: The magnetic field around a wire becomes stronger after the current has been switched off.
questions.explanation: The magnetic field disappears when the current stops flowing; it does not become stronger.

questions.question: You have an electric cell and wires but no lamp. How can you still find out whether current is flowing in the circuit?
options: Hold the wire near a lemon and see if it glows
Count the number of turns in the connecting wire
Check whether the cell has a metal cap on top
Place a compass near the wire and watch for deflection
questions.explanation: The 'Probe and ponder' question is answered by the magnetic effect: a compass needle near the wire deflects when current flows, so it can indicate current without a lamp.

questions.question: Four coils of similar shape and size are made of iron, copper, aluminium and nichrome. When current is passed, compass needles near the coils will show deflection…
options: in all four circuits
only in the iron coil circuit
only in the iron and copper coils
only in iron, copper and aluminium
questions.explanation: Any conductor carrying current produces a magnetic field around it, regardless of whether it is iron, copper, aluminium or nichrome. So the compass deflects in all four cases.

questions.question: In which year did Hans Christian Oersted discover that electricity and magnetism are linked?
questions.explanation: Oersted (1777–1851) made the discovery in 1820. 1777 and 1851 are the years of his birth and death.

questions.question: Oersted, who discovered the magnetic effect of current, was a university professor in which country?
options: Germany
England
Denmark
Italy
questions.explanation: The chapter states that Oersted was a professor at a university in Denmark. Italy is the home of Volta and Galvani.

questions.question: What did Oersted notice during a demonstration that led to his discovery?
options: A wire became hot whenever a compass was placed near it
A magnet produced a current whenever it was moved near a wire
An iron nail became a permanent magnet after the circuit was closed
A compass needle nearby deflected whenever a circuit was closed or opened
questions.explanation: While demonstrating, Oersted saw that the needle of a nearby compass deflected each time the electrical circuit was closed or opened.

questions.question: What did Oersted do before publishing his findings?
options: Investigated until he was certain current produced a magnetic field
Built the first iron-core electromagnet to prove his idea
Asked several other scientists to repeat the experiment first
Measured how much heat the current produced in the wire
questions.explanation: Oersted investigated the effect and published only when he was certain that an electric current indeed produced a magnetic field. Other scientists repeated it after he published.

questions.question: What happened after Oersted published his findings?
options: Scientists stopped studying magnets as a separate topic
Other scientists repeated his experiment to check the results
The discovery was ignored for nearly a hundred years
Volta immediately used it to build the first battery
questions.explanation: Publishing led other scientists to repeat the experiment to see if they got the same results and to investigate the electricity–magnetism link further.

questions.question: Oersted's discovery showed that electricity and magnetism, earlier thought to be unrelated, are linked.
questions.explanation: Before 1820 the two were considered separate; Oersted's observation showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field.

questions.question: Oersted discovered the magnetic effect of current in 1851 while working in Italy.
questions.explanation: The discovery was made in 1820, and Oersted worked in Denmark. 1851 is the year of his death.

questions.question: Oersted lived from 1777 to 1851. Approximately how old was he when he made his discovery in 1820?
options: About 51 years
About 74 years
About 43 years
About 31 years
questions.explanation: 1820 − 1777 = 43. He lived to about 74 (1851 − 1777), which is the tempting wrong option.

questions.question: Students doing Activity 4.1 are told they have 'made the same discovery' as Oersted. Which discovery is this?
options: An iron nail inside a coil makes a stronger magnet
A nichrome wire gets warm when current passes through
Two different metals in lemon juice give a current
A current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle
questions.explanation: Oersted's discovery was that a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, i.e. electricity and magnetism are linked. The other options are different findings in the chapter.

questions.question: Which statements about Hans Christian Oersted are correct?
options: He was a professor at a university in Denmark
He published his findings after investigating carefully
He discovered that a moving magnet produces a current
He invented the dry cell used in torches today
questions.explanation: Oersted was a Danish professor who investigated and then published that current produces a magnetic field. The idea that a moving magnet produces current is mentioned for higher grades, not credited to him; dry cells are unrelated.

questions.question: A current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is called…
options: an electromagnet
a magnetic field
a heating element
an electrolyte
questions.explanation: By definition, a current-carrying coil that behaves like a magnet is an electromagnet. A heating element produces heat; an electrolyte is the liquid in a cell.

questions.question: In Activity 4.2, what is tightly wrapped around the iron nail to make the coil?
options: A thin copper strip
Flexible insulated wire
Bare nichrome wire
A strip of chart paper
questions.explanation: About 50 cm of flexible insulated wire is wound around the nail in the form of a coil and secured with tape.

questions.question: Why does Activity 4.2 warn not to keep the wire connected to the cell for more than a few seconds?
options: The paper clips may get demagnetised
The insulation on the wire may dissolve
The cell may weaken very quickly otherwise
The nail may become permanently magnetic
questions.explanation: Keeping the coil connected for long drains the cell, so the chapter says to connect only for a few seconds or the cell may weaken quickly.

questions.question: In Activity 4.3, the paper cylinder is rolled to a diameter roughly equal to…
options: the length of a nail
the size of a lemon
the width of a compass
the width of a pencil
questions.explanation: A piece of chart paper is rolled into a cylinder about as wide as a pencil, so that an iron nail can later be inserted into it.

questions.question: About how many turns of insulated wire are wound on the paper cylinder in Activity 4.3?
options: About 50 turns
About 5 turns
About 100 turns
About 25 turns
questions.explanation: The chapter says to tightly wind around 50 turns of insulated wire on the cylinder to form a cylindrical coil.

questions.question: In Activity 4.3, when current flows through the coil WITHOUT the iron nail, the compass needles…
options: deflect only at one end of the coil
deflect, showing the coil acts as a magnet
do not move until the nail is inserted
point towards the cell's positive terminal
questions.explanation: Even without a core, the current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet and deflects the compass needles at both ends; inserting the nail only makes the deflection larger.

questions.question: What change is observed when an iron nail is inserted into the core of the current-carrying coil?
options: The coil becomes warm but not magnetic
The deflection reverses its direction
The compass needles deflect much more
The compass needles stop deflecting
questions.explanation: With an iron nail in the core the coil becomes a stronger magnet, so the deflection of the compass needles is much more and it attracts iron clips.

questions.question: Why do most practical electromagnets have an iron core?
options: It keeps the coil from getting hot
It lets the coil work without a cell
It stops the poles from reversing
It makes the electromagnet stronger
questions.explanation: An iron core makes the electromagnet much stronger, which is why most practical electromagnets include one.

questions.question: In Activity 4.3 the clips cling to the nail while current flows but fall off when it stops. This shows that the magnetism of the coil is…
options: temporary, lasting only while current flows
permanent, once the nail has been magnetised
stored in the clips rather than the coil
produced by the paper cylinder's friction
questions.explanation: The cylindrical coil loses its magnetic effect when current is stopped, so the magnetism is temporary – unlike a permanent bar magnet.

questions.question: A coil of insulated wire carrying current behaves like a magnet even without an iron nail inside it.
questions.explanation: In Activity 4.3 the coil alone deflects the compasses; the nail is inserted later only to make it stronger.

questions.question: An electromagnet keeps attracting iron clips even after the cell is disconnected.
questions.explanation: When the current is stopped, the coil loses its magnetic effect and the clips no longer cling to it.

questions.question: A coil becomes an electromagnet only when electric current flows through it.
questions.explanation: The chapter's exercise statement is true: the coil shows magnetic behaviour only while current flows; without current it is just a coil of wire.

questions.question: Which material is used for the core of the electromagnet in Activity 4.3, and why?
options: Zinc, because it forms the negative terminal
Iron, because it is a magnetic material
Copper, because it conducts electricity well
Carbon, because it forms the positive terminal
questions.explanation: An iron nail is inserted as the core; iron is a magnetic material and makes the coil a stronger magnet. Carbon and zinc are parts of a dry cell, not of an electromagnet.

questions.question: Which observations are actually made in Activity 4.3?
options: Compass needles deflect when the coil carries current
Deflection becomes much larger with an iron nail inside
Clips stay attached after the current is stopped
The coil needs two cells before any deflection appears
questions.explanation: The coil deflects the needles with one cell, and the deflection increases greatly with an iron nail. Clips fall off when current stops; a second cell is not needed for deflection.

questions.question: In Sumana's lifting-electromagnet model, what happened when she opened the circuit?
options: The battery heated up and stopped
The clips stuck more firmly to the nail
The paper clips fell off the nail
The nail became a permanent magnet
questions.explanation: Closing the circuit made the nail pick up clips like a magnet; opening it stopped the current and the clips fell off.

questions.question: Mohini and Aakarsh were surprised by Sumana's model because…
options: the nail lifted clips even after the circuit was opened
a copper nail was behaving like a magnetic material
the battery was lifting the clips without any wire
clips were attracted with no magnet present, only a circuit
questions.explanation: They had learnt that magnets attract iron, but Sumana's model had no magnet – just an iron nail, wire and battery – yet it picked up clips.

questions.question: Neha keeps the coil exactly as in Activity 4.4 but slides the iron nail out, leaving only the coiled wire. Will the coil still deflect the compass?
options: Yes, but the deflection will be less
Yes, and the deflection will be more
No, the coil cannot deflect it without the nail
Yes, and the deflection stays exactly the same
questions.explanation: A current-carrying coil is itself a magnet, so it still deflects the compass; but without the iron core it is weaker, so the deflection is less than before.

questions.question: Sumana forgets to switch OFF her lifting electromagnet. After some time the nail no longer lifts clips, though the wire is still warm. What is the most likely reason?
options: The wire's insulation melted and reversed the poles of the magnet
The cell weakened as its chemicals got used up, so the current fell
The iron nail turned into a permanent magnet and repelled the clips
The paper clips lost their magnetic property due to the warmth
questions.explanation: Leaving the circuit closed drains the cell; as its chemicals get used up the current becomes too small to make a strong magnet, though the small current still warms the wire slightly.

questions.question: How many poles does an electromagnet have?
options: Four, one at each turn
None, only a field
Two, like a bar magnet
One, unlike a bar magnet
questions.explanation: Just like a bar magnet, an electromagnet has two poles – North and South – one at each end of the coil.

questions.question: In Activity 4.4, the north pole of the compass needle is attracted towards end A of the coil. End A is therefore…
options: a north pole
not a pole
both poles
a south pole
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract. If the compass's north pole is attracted to end A, then end A must be a south pole.

questions.question: If the south pole of the compass needle is attracted towards end B of the electromagnet, end B is a…
options: north pole
south pole
neutral end
double pole
questions.explanation: Since unlike poles attract, the end that attracts the compass's south pole must be a north pole.

questions.question: After finding the polarity of end A of the electromagnet, what should you expect at end B?
options: A polarity that keeps changing
The opposite polarity to end A
The same polarity as end A
No polarity at all at end B
questions.explanation: The activity shows that the polarity of end B is opposite to that of end A – one end is north, the other south.

questions.question: When two magnets are brought close, their unlike poles (North–South)…
options: cancel each other
heat each other
attract each other
repel each other
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract each other; this fact is used to identify the poles of an electromagnet with a compass.

questions.question: Which factors can change the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Amount of current through the coil
Number of turns in the coil
Colour of the insulation on the wire
Length of the connecting wires to the switch
questions.explanation: The strength depends on the amount of current flowing through the coil and the number of turns of the coil (or both). Insulation colour and connecting-wire length are not factors mentioned.

questions.question: How can the poles of an electromagnet be reversed?
options: By adding more turns to the coil
By using a battery of more cells
By removing the iron nail from the coil
By reversing the direction of the current
questions.explanation: Changing the direction of the current reverses the poles. More turns or more cells change the strength, not the polarity.

questions.question: Using a battery of 4 cells instead of a single cell with the same coil results in…
options: a larger current and a stronger magnetic field
the same current but reversed poles
a smaller deflection of the compass
a weaker magnet that attracts fewer clips
questions.explanation: A battery with more cells gives a larger current, creating a stronger magnetic field, more deflection and more clips attracted.

questions.question: Two electromagnets use the same cell. Coil P has 50 turns and coil Q has 100 turns. Which will likely attract more clips?
options: Neither, because turns do not affect strength
Coil Q, because more turns make a stronger magnet
Coil P, because fewer turns let more current flow
Both equally, since the same cell is used
questions.explanation: Increasing the number of turns makes the coil a stronger magnet, so the 100-turn coil Q attracts more clips.

questions.question: Why does a single cell make only a weak electromagnet?
options: Its electrolyte is a paste, not a liquid
It cannot send current through a coil
It provides only a small amount of current
It has only one pole instead of two
questions.explanation: A single cell provides only a small current, so the magnetic field is weak and the coil attracts only a few clips.

questions.question: Increasing the number of turns of a coil makes an electromagnet weaker.
questions.explanation: Increasing the number of turns makes the coil a stronger magnet, not weaker.

questions.question: Changing the direction of current through an electromagnet reverses its north and south poles.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the poles of an electromagnet can be reversed by changing the direction of the current.

questions.question: An electromagnet using a single cell attracts more iron paper clips than the same electromagnet with a battery of 2 cells.
questions.explanation: A battery of 2 cells gives a larger current and a stronger field, so it attracts more clips than a single cell.

questions.question: Which statement about the strength of an electromagnet is NOT correct?
options: A battery of more cells gives a larger current than one cell
More turns on the coil make the coil a stronger magnet
An iron core inside the coil makes the magnet stronger
Using more cells reduces the deflection of the compass needle
questions.explanation: More cells give a larger current, a stronger field and MORE deflection, so the first statement is wrong. The other three are correct.

questions.question: Neha reverses the cell connections of her electromagnet. The compass needle that earlier pointed its north pole at end A will now…
options: turn its south pole towards end A
still point its north pole at end A
stop responding to the coil entirely
point towards the middle of the coil
questions.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the poles: end A changes from south to north, so now it attracts the compass's south pole. The deflection reverses.

questions.question: In 'Think like a scientist', which experiment keeps the number of cells fixed and varies another factor?
options: 4 cells with the direction reversed
2 cells with different numbers of turns
2 and 4 cells with the same coil
1 cell with the iron nail taken out
questions.explanation: Experiment (ii) uses 2 cells but changes the number of turns of the coil, so only the turns vary; experiment (i) changes the cells with the same coil.

questions.question: Which changes would make the compass deflection near an electromagnet LARGER?
options: Using a battery of more cells
Adding more turns to the coil
Reversing the direction of the current
Removing the iron nail from the coil
questions.explanation: More cells (more current) and more turns both strengthen the electromagnet. Reversing the current only reverses the poles, and removing the iron core makes it weaker.

questions.question: In the experiment '2 and 4 cells with the same coil', which variable is being changed?
options: Material of the core of the coil
Direction of current in the coil
Amount of current through the coil
Number of turns of the coil
questions.explanation: Using more cells changes the amount of current flowing through the coil; the coil (number of turns) and core are kept the same.

questions.question: Why does a freely suspended magnet rest along the north–south direction?
options: Air currents push the magnet northwards
The Sun's heat attracts the magnet's north pole
The magnet is pulled by the nearest mountain
Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet
questions.explanation: As learnt in Grade 6 and recalled here, a freely suspended magnet aligns north–south because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what creates the Earth's magnetic field?
options: Movement of liquid iron in the core producing electric currents
A giant bar magnet buried at the centre of the Earth
Solid iron mountains at the north and south poles
Lightning striking the ground repeatedly over ages
questions.explanation: Deep inside the Earth, movement of liquid iron in the core creates electric currents, which generate a magnetic field – the same link between current and magnetism seen in the activities.

questions.question: Which of the following use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate across continents and oceans?
options: Voltaic cells with two electrodes
Migratory birds, fish and animals
Lifting electromagnets in cranes
Electric kettles and heaters
questions.explanation: The 'A step further' box says many migratory birds, fish and animals use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate.

questions.question: Besides helping navigation, how does the Earth's magnetic field protect life?
options: It stops lightning from reaching the ground
It heats the core to keep the Earth warm
It blocks harmful particles coming from space
It keeps the oceans from freezing over
questions.explanation: The Earth's magnetic field acts as a shield, blocking harmful particles from space and helping protect life.

questions.question: Earth's magnetic field is produced by a huge permanent bar magnet at its centre.
questions.explanation: The field is generated by electric currents created by the movement of liquid iron in the Earth's core, not by a buried bar magnet.

questions.question: Earth's magnetic field acts as a shield against harmful particles from space.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the Earth's magnetic field blocks harmful particles from space and helps protect life on Earth.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as an application of the magnetic effect of current?
options: Electric bell
Electric fan
Electric motor
Electric kettle
questions.explanation: Electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans and loudspeakers use the magnetic effect. An electric kettle works on the heating effect.

questions.question: Which devices work on the magnetic effect of electric current?
options: Electric bell
Loudspeaker
Electric iron
Immersion rod
questions.explanation: Electric bells and loudspeakers are listed as applications of the magnetic effect; electric irons and immersion rods work on the heating effect.

questions.question: How does a crane operator control a lifting electromagnet?
options: By switching the current ON and OFF
By heating the coil with nichrome wire
By changing the shape of the iron core
By replacing the cell with a dry cell
questions.explanation: Switching current ON lifts iron/steel objects; switching it OFF makes the field disappear and releases them.

questions.question: When the current to a lifting electromagnet is switched OFF…
options: the iron objects become permanently magnetised
the magnetic field disappears and objects are released
the objects stay attached until the crane moves
the magnet becomes stronger for a few seconds
questions.explanation: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows, so switching OFF removes the field and the lifted objects drop.

questions.question: Lifting electromagnets are widely used in…
options: kitchens and bathrooms
farms and fish markets
factories and scrap yards
hospitals and schools
questions.explanation: The chapter says lifting electromagnets are widely used in factories and scrap yards to move, lift and sort heavy metal items.

questions.question: Why is an electromagnet more useful than a permanent magnet for lifting and sorting scrap iron?
options: It is always stronger than any permanent magnet
It needs no electricity supply at all to work
It attracts aluminium and copper as well as iron
Its magnetism can be switched off to release the load
questions.explanation: The key advantage is control: the operator can switch the current OFF to release objects. It needs electricity, and it attracts only magnetic materials like iron and steel.

questions.question: The chapter hints that in higher grades you will learn the 'exciting idea' that…
options: a moving magnet can also produce an electric current
a stationary magnet produces heat in a wire
a current can flow without a complete circuit
an electromagnet works without any current
questions.explanation: Just as electricity produces magnetism, a moving magnet can lead to an electric current – the basis of power generators.

questions.question: The deep connection between electricity and magnetism forms the basis of devices such as…
options: immersion rods and hair dryers
electric motors and power generators
lemon cells and zinc dry cells
electric irons and electric kettles
questions.explanation: Motors and generators rely on the electricity–magnetism link; cells work on chemical reactions and irons/kettles on the heating effect.

questions.question: The special wire tied between the nails in Activity 4.5 is made of…
options: aluminium
iron
nichrome
copper
questions.explanation: Activity 4.5 uses a nichrome wire, which offers higher resistance than copper and so heats noticeably.

questions.question: In Activity 4.5, the nichrome wire used is about…
options: 3 mm thick and 10 cm long
0.3 mm thick and 100 cm long
0.6 mm thick and 5 cm long
0.3 mm thick and 10 cm long
questions.explanation: The chapter specifies a nichrome wire of thickness about 0.3 mm (26–28 gauge) and length 10 cm.

questions.question: Why does the nichrome wire become warm when current flows through it?
options: Its resistance converts some electrical energy into heat
The cell pumps hot chemicals along the wire to warm it
The magnetic field around the wire rubs against the air
The nails act as heating elements that warm the wire
questions.explanation: A conductor opposes (resists) the flow of current; this resistance causes some electrical energy to be converted into heat energy.

questions.question: Compared with a copper wire of the same size and length, a nichrome wire…
options: offers the same resistance
offers higher resistance
offers lower resistance
offers no resistance at all
questions.explanation: Different conductors offer different resistance; nichrome offers higher resistance than copper of the same size and length, so it heats more.

questions.question: The warming of a conductor when electric current passes through it is called the…
options: chemical effect of electric current
lighting effect of electric current
heating effect of electric current
magnetic effect of electric current
questions.explanation: Generation of heat in a conductor due to the flow of current is the heating effect of electric current.

questions.question: Activity 4.5 is repeated with a battery of 2 cells instead of 1 for the same duration. The nichrome wire…
options: heats up less because the cells share the load
heats up the same since the wire is unchanged
does not heat at all as the cells cancel out
heats up more because the current is larger
questions.explanation: More heat is generated with 2 cells because the heat produced depends on the magnitude of the current, which is larger with 2 cells.

questions.question: On which of these does the heat generated in a wire depend?
options: Material of the wire
Duration for which current flows
Colour of the wire's insulation
Direction of the current
questions.explanation: Heat generated depends on the material, thickness and length of the wire, the current and the duration of flow. Insulation colour and current direction are not factors.

questions.question: Select the factors that affect how much heat a current-carrying wire produces.
options: Length of the wire
Magnitude of the current
Direction of the current
Number of compasses placed nearby
questions.explanation: The chapter lists material, thickness, length, duration and magnitude of current. Direction of current affects poles of an electromagnet, not heating; compasses merely detect fields.

questions.question: Which statement about the heating effect of current is NOT correct?
options: Only nichrome wire gets heated when current flows through it
Different conductors offer different resistance to current
Heat generated depends on how long the current flows
An incandescent lamp glows because its filament is heated
questions.explanation: Any conductor carrying current gets heated, since every conductor offers some resistance; nichrome simply heats more. The other statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: While making the electromagnet, students noticed the wire ends got warm. This is because…
options: the paper clips rub against the wire ends and warm them
the wire's resistance converts some energy to heat
the magnetic field heats up the surrounding air
the iron nail transfers its heat to the wire
questions.explanation: Even ordinary connecting wire has some resistance, so current passing through it produces heat – the heating effect accompanies the magnetic effect.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say to touch the nichrome wire only 'momentarily' and not hold it?
options: To avoid draining the cell faster
To avoid shocking the compass
To avoid injury from the heated wire
To avoid demagnetising the wire
questions.explanation: The safety note says not to touch the wire for an extended period, because the heated wire can cause injury.

questions.question: Two nichrome wires of equal length, one twice as thick as the other, are connected one by one to the same cell for 30 s. The heat produced in them…
options: will be equal, because both wires are made of nichrome
will be equal, because both carry current for 30 seconds
will be zero, because thick wires have no resistance
will differ, because heat depends on the wire's thickness
questions.explanation: Heat generated depends on material, thickness, length and duration. Same material and time but different thickness means the heating will differ.

questions.question: Electrical energy is converted into heat because a conductor offers resistance to the flow of current.
questions.explanation: Resistance to the flow of current causes some electrical energy to be converted into heat energy in the conductor.

questions.question: A copper wire offers higher resistance than a nichrome wire of the same size and length.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: nichrome offers higher resistance than copper of the same size and length.

questions.question: An incandescent lamp glows because…
options: its filament is heated by the electric current
its filament becomes a magnet and glows
the gas inside burns like a candle flame
chemical reactions in the glass give light
questions.explanation: As learnt in Grade 7, the filament is heated by the current until it glows – an example of the heating effect.

questions.question: In Grade 7 the torch lamp sometimes got warm while glowing with an electric cell. Which effect explains this?
options: Attraction between the lamp and the cell
Heating effect of current in the filament
Magnetic effect of current in the filament
Chemical effect of the cell's electrolyte
questions.explanation: The filament resists the current and converts electrical energy into heat, which is why the lamp glows and feels warm.

questions.question: A current flows through a nichrome wire for a short time. (i) The wire becomes warm. (ii) A compass placed below the wire deflects. Which option is correct?
options: Only (ii) is correct
Neither (i) nor (ii) is correct
Both (i) and (ii) are correct
Only (i) is correct
questions.explanation: Any current-carrying conductor shows both effects: nichrome's resistance makes it warm (heating effect) and the current produces a magnetic field that deflects the compass (magnetic effect).

questions.question: Nichrome wire is commonly used in electrical heating devices because it…
options: is a good conductor of electricity
is cheaper than copper wire of same size
is a perfect insulator of electricity
generates more heat for a given current
questions.explanation: Nichrome offers higher resistance than copper, so it generates more heat for a given current – ideal for heating elements. It is a conductor, not an insulator, and cost is not the reason given.

questions.question: Which part of an electric heater, iron or kettle actually produces the heat?
options: The heating element
The magnetic core
The electrolyte paste
The compass needle
questions.explanation: All these appliances contain a rod or coil of wire called a heating element, which gets hot when current flows.

questions.question: A heating element is best described as…
options: a zinc container with a carbon rod
a rod or coil of wire that gets hot
a glass container with two rods
a coil wound around an iron nail
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the heating element as a rod or coil of wire; the other options describe a Voltaic cell, an electromagnet and a dry cell.

questions.question: In some appliances the heating element can be seen glowing red hot. This shows that…
options: the chemicals in the element are burning
the element has lost all its resistance
a large amount of heat is produced by the current
the element has become a strong magnet
questions.explanation: The red glow is due to the heating effect – the element becomes so hot that it glows, like a lamp filament.

questions.question: Which of these appliances work on the heating effect of electric current?
options: Electric iron
Hair dryer
Electric bell
Loudspeaker
Electric motor
questions.explanation: Electric irons and hair dryers are listed with heaters, stoves, kettles and immersion rods as heating-effect appliances; bells, loudspeakers and motors use the magnetic effect.

questions.question: Select the devices that contain a heating element.
options: Electric kettle
Immersion rod
Electric fan
Electromagnet crane
questions.explanation: Kettles and water-heating immersion rods have heating elements; fans and lifting electromagnets work on the magnetic effect.

questions.question: Which device does NOT belong with the other three?
options: Electric stove
Electric kettle
Electric iron
Electric fan
questions.explanation: Stoves, kettles and irons work on the heating effect; an electric fan works on the magnetic effect of current.

questions.question: What problem can the heating effect cause when electricity is transmitted through wires?
options: Energy loss in the wires
Reversal of the magnetic poles
Faster charging of batteries
Melting of the electrolyte
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that the heating effect can cause energy loss in wires during transmission.

questions.question: Overheating in appliances may lead to…
options: the wires losing their resistance completely
melted plastic in plugs and sockets, or even fires
the appliance becoming a permanent magnet
the cell inside the appliance becoming recharged
questions.explanation: Overheating may damage plugs and sockets, melting plastic parts, or even lead to fires.

questions.question: What is placed in household circuits to minimise incidents caused by overheating?
options: Spare dry cells
Iron nail cores
Safety devices
Extra switches
questions.explanation: Household circuits include safety devices to minimise damage from overheating.

questions.question: To prevent unnecessary heating in switchboards, wires, plugs and sockets should be…
options: made of nichrome to resist the heat
wrapped tightly around an iron core
kept dipped in a weak salt solution
rated for the current of the connection
questions.explanation: Appropriate wires, plugs and sockets rated for the specified current of the connections prevent unnecessary heating.

questions.question: In steel-manufacturing industries, the heating effect of electric current is used to…
options: melt and recycle scrap steel in a furnace
magnetise steel rods for lifting cranes
charge large lithium-ion batteries
separate zinc containers from carbon rods
questions.explanation: A high-temperature furnace uses electric current to produce heat that melts and recycles scrap steel into usable steel.

questions.question: The chapter describes a furnace as…
options: a device that detects magnetic fields
an enclosed space built to generate heat
a coil of wire wound on an iron nail
a container holding an electrolyte
questions.explanation: A furnace is defined in the text as an enclosed space built to generate heat.

questions.question: Overheating can melt the plastic parts of plugs and sockets.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that overheating may damage plugs and sockets, where plastic parts may melt.

questions.question: The heating effect of current is always useful and never causes any problems.
questions.explanation: It is useful in appliances but can also cause energy loss in transmission, damage to plugs and sockets, and fires.

questions.question: A thin wire rated for a small current is used to connect a high-current room heater. What is the likely consequence?
options: The heater will produce less heat than normal
The wire will become a permanent magnet
The wire may overheat and its insulation may melt
The heater will work as an electromagnet instead
questions.explanation: Wires not rated for the current heat up unnecessarily; the chapter warns that this can melt plastic parts or cause fires.

questions.question: Another name for a Voltaic cell is a…
options: Lithium cell
Carbon cell
Nichrome cell
Galvanic cell
questions.explanation: A Voltaic cell is also known as a Galvanic cell, after the Italian scientists Volta and Galvani.

questions.question: The solution used in a Voltaic cell is called the…
options: electrolyte
electrode
conductor
insulator
questions.explanation: The liquid in the cell, usually a weak acid or salt solution, is the electrolyte; the metal rods are electrodes.

questions.question: The metal rods partly dipped in the liquid of a Voltaic cell are called…
options: filaments
electrodes
electrolytes
elements
questions.explanation: The two metal rods are electrodes. The liquid is the electrolyte; a filament is part of a lamp; a heating element is in a heater.

questions.question: What produces the electricity in a Voltaic cell?
options: A magnetic field created by the two metal rods
Friction between the liquid and the container
A chemical reaction between rods and electrolyte
Heat from the rods warming the electrolyte
questions.explanation: A chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte produces electricity – a cell generates current because of chemical reactions inside it.

questions.question: The two electrodes in a Voltaic cell must be…
options: made of the same metal
both made of carbon rods
fully dipped in the liquid
made of different materials
questions.explanation: The cell contains two metal rods made of different materials, partly (not fully) dipped in the electrolyte.

questions.question: The electrolyte in a Voltaic cell is usually…
options: a weak acid or a salt solution
pure distilled drinking water
a thick moist carbon paste
melted iron from the core
questions.explanation: The electrolyte is usually a weak acid or salt solution. A thick paste is used in dry cells, not Voltaic cells.

questions.question: When a Voltaic cell is connected in a circuit, electric current flows through the circuit from…
options: both terminals towards the centre
the positive terminal to the negative terminal
the negative terminal to the positive terminal
the electrolyte directly into the lamp
questions.explanation: The chapter states that current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal.

questions.question: Why does a Voltaic cell eventually become 'dead'?
options: The electrolyte freezes solid
The current reverses direction
The chemicals inside get used up
The electrodes become magnetised
questions.explanation: Over time the chemicals get used up, the cell stops working and cannot supply any more electricity – it is then called dead.

questions.question: Volta and Galvani, after whom Voltaic and Galvanic cells are named, were scientists from…
options: Denmark
France
Germany
Italy
questions.explanation: Both Alessandro Volta and Luigi Galvani were Italian scientists; Oersted was from Denmark.

questions.question: What did Galvani observe in the late 1700s?
options: A frog's leg kicked when touched by two different metals
A compass needle moved when a circuit nearby was closed
A wire grew warm when copper and iron were connected
A piece of iron became magnetic when placed in a coil
questions.explanation: Galvani noticed that a dead frog's leg kicked when touched with two different metals – copper and iron.

questions.question: Galvani believed the electricity that made the frog's leg kick came from…
options: the air around
the frog itself
the two metals
the salt water
questions.explanation: Galvani thought the electricity came from the frog; Volta disagreed and argued it came from the metals.

questions.question: Volta's view was that the electricity came from…
options: the glass of the container
the heat of the wires
the metals, not the frog
the frog's leg muscles
questions.explanation: Volta believed the electricity came from the metals and not from the frog, and tested this idea.

questions.question: How did Volta test his idea about the source of the electricity?
options: He used two rods of the same metal and got a larger current
He heated the frog's leg and measured its kicking
He placed a compass near the frog and watched it deflect
He used saltwater-soaked paper instead of the frog's leg
questions.explanation: Volta replaced the frog's leg with saltwater-soaked paper and still got a current, proving the frog was not the source.

questions.question: Volta's experiment showed that the electric current was generated by…
options: a combination of metals and a liquid
the muscles of a living animal
friction between two metal rods
the magnetic field of the Earth
questions.explanation: Getting a current with metals and saltwater-soaked paper showed that the combination of metals and liquid generated the current – leading to the first battery.

questions.question: Volta's experiment with saltwater-soaked paper led to the invention of the first battery.
questions.explanation: Showing that metals plus a liquid produce current led Volta to invent the first battery.

questions.question: Galvani correctly concluded that the electricity came from the two metals rather than the frog.
questions.explanation: Galvani thought the electricity came from the frog; it was Volta who concluded it came from the metals.

questions.question: Which statement about a Voltaic cell is NOT correct?
options: It stops working once the chemicals are used up
Its electrodes are fully submerged in the electrolyte
It uses two rods made of different materials
Its electrolyte is usually a weak acid or salt solution
questions.explanation: The electrodes are only partly dipped in the electrolyte, not fully submerged. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: Which statements about Volta and Galvani are correct?
options: Galvani thought the electricity came from the frog
Volta showed that metals plus a liquid produce current
Galvani invented the first battery
Volta worked as a professor in Denmark
questions.explanation: Galvani credited the frog; Volta disproved this with saltwater-soaked paper and invented the first battery. Both were Italian; Denmark is Oersted's country.

questions.question: Match: which description fits a Voltaic cell?
options: Works on heating effect of current
Best suited for electric heater
Works on chemical reactions
Works on magnetic effect of current
questions.explanation: A Voltaic cell generates current through chemical reactions; the electromagnet uses the magnetic effect, the iron the heating effect, and nichrome suits heaters.

questions.question: In the lemon cell of Activity 4.6, what are the two electrodes?
options: Zinc rod and carbon rod
Copper wire and zinc strip
Iron nail and carbon rod
Copper wire and iron nail
questions.explanation: A copper wire/strip and an iron nail are inserted into each lemon as the two metal electrodes.

questions.question: What acts as the electrolyte in the lemon cell?
options: Lemon juice
Copper wire
Iron nail
Lemon peel
questions.explanation: The lemon juice is the electrolyte which helps conduct electricity between the copper and iron electrodes.

questions.question: In Activity 4.6, the LED is connected between…
options: the copper wire and iron nail of one single lemon
copper wire of the first lemon and iron nail of the last
the copper wires of the first lemon and the last lemon
the iron nails of the first lemon and the last lemon
questions.explanation: The LED is connected between the copper wire of the first lemon and the iron nail of the last lemon, after joining the copper wires and nails of neighbouring lemons.

questions.question: If the LED does not glow at first in the lemon-cell activity, what should you do?
options: Squeeze the lemons until juice flows
Replace the iron nails with zinc
Reverse the LED's connections
Add more copper wires to each lemon
questions.explanation: The chapter says: if the LED does not glow, reverse its connections – an LED passes current only in one direction.

questions.question: Why might reversing the LED's connections make it glow?
options: Reversing warms the lemon juice and frees charge
The LED needs a few seconds to charge up fully
The copper and iron swap roles when reversed
Current passes through an LED only in one direction
questions.explanation: Current can pass through the LED only when its longer (positive) wire is connected to the positive terminal and the shorter to the negative; reversing fixes a wrong connection.

questions.question: The longer wire of an LED must be connected to…
options: the positive terminal of the battery
the negative terminal of the battery
the iron nail of the first lemon
the middle lemon in the chain
questions.explanation: The longer wire is the LED's positive terminal and goes to the battery's positive terminal; the shorter wire goes to the negative terminal.

questions.question: A glowing LED in Activity 4.6 indicates that…
options: the circuit is broken
the lemon cell is working
the LED is overheating
the lemons are magnetic
questions.explanation: The chapter says a glowing LED indicates that your cell is working, i.e. it is producing current.

questions.question: Instead of lemon juice, what else can be used as the electrolyte in a home-made cell?
options: Cooking oils
Melted candle wax
Salt solutions
Pure water only
questions.explanation: The chapter says you may also use salt solutions instead of lemon juice; a weak acid or salt solution is the usual electrolyte.

questions.question: Cell (a) has an iron nail and copper strip in lemon juice; cell (b) has the same electrodes in pure water. When the switch is closed, the LED will glow…
options: only in (b), because pure water is cleaner
in both, because the metals are the same
in neither, because an LED needs a dry cell
only in (a), because lemon juice is an electrolyte
questions.explanation: A cell needs an electrolyte (weak acid or salt solution) to conduct and react with the electrodes. Lemon juice does this; pure water is not listed as an electrolyte, so (b) gives no current.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a common metal pair for Voltaic cells?
options: Zinc and copper
Iron and aluminium
Lead and magnesium
Silver and copper
questions.explanation: Listed pairs are zinc/copper, zinc/silver, aluminium/copper, iron/copper, magnesium/copper and lead/copper. Each pair includes copper or zinc.

questions.question: Which metal is given as an example of one that acts as a positive electrode?
options: Nickel
Copper
Zinc
Cobalt
questions.explanation: The chapter says metals like copper act as positive electrodes, while metals like zinc act as negative electrodes.

questions.question: Which metal is given as an example of one that acts as a negative electrode?
options: Silver
Cobalt
Zinc
Copper
questions.explanation: Zinc is the example of a negative electrode; copper is the example of a positive electrode.

questions.question: Lemon juice helps conduct electricity and acts as the electrolyte in the lemon cell.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that the electrolyte is the lemon juice, which helps conduct electricity.

questions.question: In the lemon cell, the copper wire and the iron nail must touch each other inside the lemon.
questions.explanation: The copper wire and iron nail are inserted keeping them apart by a small distance; they must not touch.

questions.question: Which of these are listed in the chapter as common metal pairs for Voltaic cells?
options: Magnesium/copper
Lead/copper
Copper/copper
Nichrome/iron
questions.explanation: Magnesium/copper and lead/copper are listed. The two electrodes must be different materials, so copper/copper is not valid; nichrome/iron is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why are dry cells called 'dry'?
options: They contain no electrolyte of any kind inside
They must be stored in a dry place when unused
Their electrodes are made of dried carbon powder
The electrolyte is a thick paste, not a liquid
questions.explanation: They are called dry because the electrolyte is not a liquid but a thick moist paste. They do still contain an electrolyte.

questions.question: In a dry cell, the zinc container acts as the…
options: negative terminal
positive terminal
electrolyte
metal cap
questions.explanation: The zinc container is the negative terminal; the carbon rod with its metal cap is the positive terminal.

questions.question: The carbon rod at the centre of a dry cell, covered with a metal cap, acts as the…
options: zinc container
positive terminal
negative terminal
electrolyte paste
questions.explanation: The carbon rod covered with a metal cap is the positive terminal of the dry cell.

questions.question: What surrounds the carbon rod inside a dry cell?
options: A coil of copper wire
A layer of lemon juice
A paste-like electrolyte
A liquid weak acid
questions.explanation: The carbon rod is surrounded by the paste-like electrolyte, which is why the cell is called 'dry'.

questions.question: A dry cell is described as a single-use cell. This means…
options: it can be used by only one person
it works for exactly one hour
it can be recharged only once
once used up it has to be disposed of
questions.explanation: Single use means that once the dry cell is used up it cannot be recharged and must be disposed of.

questions.question: Dry cells are less portable compared to Voltaic cells.
questions.explanation: Voltaic cells with liquid electrolytes are inconvenient; dry cells with paste electrolytes are far more portable and are the most widely used cells today.

questions.question: Which parts of a dry cell play the role that the two electrodes play in a Voltaic cell?
options: Zinc container and carbon rod
The metal cap and the paste
The paste and the outer case
The carbon rod and the paste
questions.explanation: The zinc container (negative) and the carbon rod (positive) are the two terminals/electrodes; the paste is the electrolyte.

questions.question: Which statement about dry cells is NOT correct?
options: The carbon rod is at the centre of the cell
The dry cell can be recharged many times
The zinc container is the negative terminal
The electrolyte is a thick moist paste
questions.explanation: A dry cell is single-use and must be disposed of once used up; it cannot be recharged. The other statements describe its structure correctly.

questions.question: Why are dry cells more widely used today than Voltaic cells?
options: They produce a stronger magnetic field
They use lemon juice which is cheap
They are more convenient for everyday use
They never run out and need no disposal
questions.explanation: Voltaic cells were important but not convenient for everyday use; dry cells, with a paste electrolyte, are convenient and widely used.

questions.question: In a dry cell the zinc container is the negative terminal and the carbon rod is the positive terminal.
questions.explanation: This matches the structure described in the chapter and Fig. 4.9.

questions.question: A dry cell uses a liquid weak acid as its electrolyte, just like a Voltaic cell.
questions.explanation: A dry cell's electrolyte is a thick moist paste, not a liquid – that is the whole point of the name 'dry'.

questions.question: Which statements about dry cells are correct?
options: They are one of the most widely used cells today
Their electrolyte is a thick moist paste
They can be recharged by connecting to a charger
Their outer container is made of copper
questions.explanation: Dry cells are widely used and have a paste electrolyte. They are single-use (not rechargeable) and their container is zinc, not copper.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of rechargeable batteries?
options: They never wear out even after years
They do not contain any chemicals
They are lighter than all dry cells
They can be recharged and reused many times
questions.explanation: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times, preventing wastage; but they do wear out slowly.

questions.question: Using rechargeable batteries helps by…
options: preventing wastage and saving money over time
producing heat for household appliances
generating magnetic fields for cranes
working forever without needing a charger
questions.explanation: Reusing a battery many times prevents wastage and saves money over time, according to the chapter.

questions.question: Why does a phone battery need charging more often after a year or two?
options: The charger gradually loses its magnetic effect
The battery slowly wears out after being charged many times
The phone's screen uses more energy as the phone gets older
The electrolyte inside turns from a paste into a liquid
questions.explanation: Rechargeable batteries do not last forever; after being charged and used many times they slowly wear out, so they hold less charge.

questions.question: Which is the most common type of rechargeable battery today?
options: Lemon cell battery
Voltaic cell battery
Lithium-ion battery
Dry cell battery
questions.explanation: The lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery is the most common rechargeable battery, found in almost all battery-powered devices.

questions.question: Lithium-ion batteries rely on special metals such as…
options: zinc and carbon
copper and iron
nichrome and lead
lithium and cobalt
questions.explanation: Li-ion batteries use lithium and cobalt; zinc and carbon are dry-cell materials, copper and iron are lemon-cell electrodes.

questions.question: Why are countries racing to secure supplies and recycle old batteries?
options: Lithium and cobalt are mined only in limited regions
Rechargeable batteries are the only source of magnetism
Dry cells have completely stopped being manufactured
Recycled batteries charge faster than brand-new ones
questions.explanation: Lithium and cobalt are mined and processed in limited parts of the world, so countries race to secure supplies, recycle and develop new technologies.

questions.question: What do solid-state batteries replace?
options: The lithium inside them with cheaper iron rods
Liquid or paste electrolytes with solid materials
The metal electrodes with solid plastic rods
The charging cable with a built-in solar panel
questions.explanation: Solid-state batteries replace the liquid or paste-like electrolytes with solid materials.

questions.question: Which advantages are expected from future solid-state batteries?
options: Much safer
Charge faster
Never need to be replaced
Work without any electrolyte
questions.explanation: They are expected to be safer, charge faster and last longer. They still use an electrolyte (a solid one) and 'last longer' does not mean never replaced.

questions.question: Which of these is listed in the chapter as using rechargeable batteries?
options: Immersion rod
Electric stove
Inverter
Electric kettle
questions.explanation: Rechargeable batteries are shown in laptops, phones, cameras, inverters and vehicles; kettles, rods and stoves are heating appliances.

questions.question: Which statement about rechargeable batteries is NOT correct?
options: They can be reused multiple times
They slowly wear out after many uses
They power laptops and electric vehicles
They last forever if charged properly
questions.explanation: Rechargeable batteries also do not last forever – they wear out slowly after many charge cycles. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call improved rechargeable batteries 'very important' for the future?
options: They support the move to environmentally friendly power
They will replace all electromagnets in factories
They make lifting cranes lift heavier scrap
They produce more heat than nichrome elements
questions.explanation: Better rechargeable batteries matter as the world moves to developing environmentally friendly sources of electrical power.

questions.question: Rechargeable batteries also wear out slowly after being charged and used many times.
questions.explanation: The chapter says rechargeable batteries do not last forever and slowly wear out after many charges.

questions.question: Solid-state batteries use a thick moist paste as their electrolyte.
questions.explanation: Solid-state batteries replace liquid or paste electrolytes with solid materials; the paste is used in dry cells.

questions.question: Lithium-ion batteries are found only in electric vehicles.
questions.explanation: Li-ion batteries are found in almost all devices that use batteries – phones, laptops, cameras and more, not only vehicles.

questions.question: Can all cells and batteries be recharged?
options: Yes, if the electrolyte is a paste
No, dry cells are single-use
Yes, every cell can be recharged
No, only Voltaic cells can be
questions.explanation: Dry cells are single-use and must be disposed of when used up; only rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused.

questions.question: A battery that has stopped working may still contain…
options: a strong permanent magnet made of iron and nickel
clean water and a long coil of insulated copper wire
acids and metals such as lead, cadmium or lithium
fresh electrolyte that can be poured into a new cell
questions.explanation: Even a 'dead' battery can contain acids and metals like lead, cadmium, nickel or lithium, which can be harmful or valuable.

questions.question: Why should used batteries not be thrown in regular garbage?
options: They may recharge themselves in the garbage heap
They make the garbage pile magnetic and hard to move
They are needed later to power the garbage trucks
Their materials may cause fires or harm the environment
questions.explanation: The acids and metals inside may cause fires or be harmful to the environment if thrown in regular garbage.

questions.question: Where does the chapter say used batteries should be disposed of?
options: At special e-waste recycling facilities
In the kitchen compost bin with food scraps
In a nearby river or lake far from houses
In the regular household garbage bin
questions.explanation: Many places have special e-waste recycling facilities where used batteries can be disposed of safely.

questions.question: Why is recycling batteries described as good for the planet and the people?
options: Recycling makes the batteries magnetic again
Valuable materials are reused and harm is avoided
Old batteries become stronger after recycling
Recycled batteries never need charging again
questions.explanation: Many battery materials are valuable and can be recycled and reused, while keeping harmful acids and metals out of the environment.

questions.question: The chapter says a battery that stops working is 'not completely dead'. What does this mean?
options: It will start working again after resting for a day
It keeps a magnetic field even without current
It still holds chemicals and metals, harmful or valuable
It can be shaken to make it supply current again
questions.explanation: 'Not completely dead' refers to the acids and metals still inside, which can cause harm if dumped or be recovered by recycling – not to the battery working again.

questions.question: Many materials used in batteries are valuable and can be recycled and reused.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that many battery materials are valuable and could be recycled and reused.

questions.question: It is safe to throw used batteries in regular garbage because they are completely dead.
questions.explanation: Used batteries still contain acids and metals that may cause fires or harm the environment; they should go to e-waste facilities.

questions.question: Which metals does the chapter mention as possibly present in a used battery?
options: Lead
Cadmium
Copper
Nichrome
questions.explanation: Lead, cadmium, nickel and lithium are named. Copper is a lemon-cell electrode and nichrome a heating wire, not listed as battery waste.

questions.question: If you are not sure how to dispose of a used battery, the chapter advises you to…
options: bury it in the garden
burn it in a furnace
put it in a lemon
ask your teacher
questions.explanation: The chapter says: if you are not sure, ask your teacher – and use e-waste recycling facilities.
